Chapter 4: Moral Dilemmas and the Complexity of Survival
When you think about surviving in Auschwitz, you might picture a battle of sheer physical endurance. But the reality? It was so much more than that. Every day, people faced choices that tested not only their bodies, but their deepest values. Imagine—being forced to ask yourself, how far would I go to survive? What could I live with giving up, and where would I finally draw the line?
Food was at the center of so many of these tough decisions. The rations were barely enough to keep anyone alive. So, what do you do? Some ended up stealing, or trading whatever they could for just a bit more to eat. Others risked sneaking scraps from the kitchen, knowing full well that getting caught meant harsh punishment. The line between survival and betrayal? It was razor thin. And for many, the choices they made haunted them long after.
Relationships inside the camp were shaped by this constant pressure. Trust was hard to come by. Betrayal could hit from any direction. Picture sharing your last piece of bread with someone you consider a friend, only to find yourself alone when you need help most. Some people teamed up out of necessity, knowing loyalty was a luxury they simply couldn’t afford. Still, you’d be surprised—acts of kindness did happen. A few risked their own safety, maybe by sneaking medicine to someone in need or quietly passing on information about the next selection.
The way the camp was run made everything more complicated. If you cooperated with the authorities—say, by informing on someone or enforcing their rules—you might get a better job or an extra ration. For some, that was the only way to survive. For others, it felt like a betrayal of everything they believed in. The camp forced people to weigh their own desperate needs against the suffering of those around them. There simply weren’t any easy answers.
Then there was the challenge of illness and injury. The camp’s infirmary might sound like a place to recover, but really, it was a last resort. Often, it was just a waiting room for death. Still, some managed to get a spot there—maybe by luck, or by convincing someone they were useful. Sometimes, this meant a break from the hardest labor, but it also meant leaving friends behind, and never escaping the fear of the next selection.
And every time new prisoners arrived, it was a stark reminder of how quickly things could change. The ones who’d survived for months or even years watched as new faces struggled to find their footing, making mistakes that could be fatal. Some tried to help, sharing advice or whatever lessons they’d picked up. Others kept their distance, knowing that getting too attached only brought more risk.
When you look at life in Auschwitz through this lens, it’s clear—survival was never just about enduring the physical hardship. It was a constant struggle with impossible choices, and the moral cost of staying alive was sometimes the heaviest burden of all.
